The Upstream Problem

The failure isn't in the model.
It's in the meeting before the model was approved.

These are not data quality problems. They are not talent problems. They are not vendor problems. They are upstream problems.

In every failed initiative, the same thing was skipped: someone defining precisely which business problem the AI must solve, for whom, and how you will know when it worked. That is problem formulation. It is the least glamorous skill in the building. It is also the one that determines everything.

I have seen this across 20+ years in quantitative finance — at Merrill Lynch, Millennium, Point72, Soros. A model on the wrong problem does not produce a bad slide deck. It produces a loss. The cost of a wrong AI initiative in a Fortune 500 company is the same kind of event. It just moves slower.

At Future Alpha 2026 — a room of quants, portfolio managers, CIOs, and heads of risk — the most-requested talk was not about architecture. It was about how to state a problem clearly.

The Situations We Walk Into

We know what your last six months looked like.

The pilot that never left the room.

Your team ran a proof of concept. It worked in the demo. The data scientists were proud. Then someone asked what system it would actually run on. Who would maintain it. Whether the compliance team had signed off. The project went quiet. Three months later, someone filed it under "learnings."

The board asked a question you couldn't answer.

They didn't ask about the model. They asked: what does this produce for us, by when, and how will we know? You had three answers. None of them were the same. The meeting ended. A follow-up was scheduled. The follow-up was rescheduled.

The initiative that had five sponsors and no owner.

Legal said maybe. Finance said not yet. IT said they needed six months. The business unit said they needed it now. Everyone was right. No one was in charge. It is still happening, technically. No one talks about it at the weekly.

The vendor who sold you a solution before hearing the problem.

They came in with a demo. The demo was impressive. You signed the contract. Six months later, the tool was doing exactly what it was designed to do — just not for the problem your organization actually had.

"The hype on LinkedIn says everything has changed, but in our operations, nothing fundamental has shifted."

— COO, mid-market manufacturing firm. MIT Project NANDA research.

The Decision Intelligence Spectrum

What it looks like when the upstream problem is solved first.

When an organization gets the problem formulation right, everything downstream becomes easier. The data team builds the right thing. The board gets answers they can act on.

All Human Augmented Intelligence All Machine

Brain-Driven

Pure intuition, no data. Fast and confident — frequently wrong in complex systems.

Data-Informed  ←  The goal

Human judgment shaped by relevant data, not replaced by it. Use what is useful. Discard what is not.

Data-Driven

Outputs without judgment. When the model is wrong — and eventually it is — no one knows how to course-correct.

The diagram maps four positions. At one end: Brain-Driven — pure intuition, no data. At the other: Data-Driven — pure automation, no judgment. In between is Data-Informed — where human judgment is shaped by relevant data, not replaced by it. Above all three sits Augmented Intelligence.

What lifts an organization there is a state GIDS calls Cognitive Clarity: knowing exactly what your AI should do, why, and how you will measure whether it worked — the state the Assess phase exists to create.

The A.I.R. Framework™

Most AI consultants sell you implementation.
We sell you the conversation that comes before it.

Most AI initiatives start with the solution. A timeline is set. A vendor is selected. Then someone asks what problem this solves. The answer is not specific enough. But the timeline is locked. So everyone moves forward.

This is not incompetence. It is the default setting of any organization under pressure to "do AI."

Hover each phase to explore →

A.I.R. Framework™ · U.S. Copyright Registered

Assess

Organizational Readiness

Where everything begins — before any tool is selected, before any budget is approved. It asks one question:

"Can you describe your AI initiative in one sentence that a smart, non-technical colleague would push back on?"

Implement

Evidence-Based Deployment

What happens when Assess is done. Not before. When you know exactly what you are building, for whom, and how success is measured, implementation is disciplined execution — not an expensive experiment.

Revolve

Continuous Optimization

The discipline most enterprises skip. AI that does not continuously improve becomes a liability. Revolve closes the loop: systematic review, adaptation, and documented learning.

Deploy →
Optimize →
← Evaluate

The organization that wins is not the one with the best model. It is the one that asked the right question first.

Supported by the major studies on enterprise AI failure published in the last three years.

The Engagement

What a GIDS engagement looks like.
And what it is not.

What it is.

A Feasibility Assessment begins with one question: can you describe your AI initiative in a single sentence a colleague would push back on?

The 5-Step Assessment covers data readiness, stakeholder alignment, use case clarity, ROI definition, and deployment risk.

The output is a board-ready feasibility report — exactly what is ready, what is not, and what to do before anyone writes a line of code.

Most organizations use this report to stop a project that would have failed — or to accelerate one held back by the wrong concerns.

What it is not.

GIDS does not build AI systems.

GIDS does not manage your data infrastructure.

GIDS does not replace your data team.

GIDS does not validate decisions already made.

GIDS is not a fit if you need a vendor to confirm a direction already chosen.

FAQ

Questions we hear in every first meeting.

Your data science team builds models. GIDS determines whether the model should be built at all — and whether the problem it is solving is the right problem. Those are different disciplines. Most failed AI initiatives had a competent data team. What they did not have was someone asking the upstream question before the build started.
The average failed enterprise AI initiative takes 18 months and several million dollars before someone asks what a GIDS assessment asks in the first conversation. The assessment does not slow your initiative down. It finds out whether your current timeline is pointed at the right target.
You can. Most organizations do. Then they spend 12 months building something that fails when it meets the real organization — the compliance team that was not in the room, the legacy system that cannot support the output, the three departments that agreed in principle and disagreed in practice. Assess first. Build second.
Most AI consultants arrive with a methodology and adapt your problem to fit it. GIDS starts with your problem. If a prior engagement delivered a framework but not a decision you could act on, that is exactly the gap the A.I.R. Framework is designed to fill. It is a diagnostic tool, not a template.
A board-ready feasibility report. It states clearly what your organization is ready to build, what it is not ready to build, and what must happen before any build begins. It is written in plain language. The board can read it. The CFO can read it. The General Counsel can read it. That is the point.
Request the assessment. John reviews your situation before the call and will tell you whether GIDS is the right fit. If it is not, he will tell you what is. There is no cost to finding out. There is often a significant cost to not finding out.
